title: Her first Capitol contract: flat fee and promised royalty
summary: Her first Capitol contract was non-royalty, a flat fee per record with a promised royalty if it hit, before Carlos Gastel became her manager.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, but when you first started
recording you did have an agreement that you would get royalties.
Well, frankly, some of the things, yes, I did. However, my very first contract with Capitol, for instance, was a non-royalty contract. However, this was a temporary contract. This was --
How many records did you do under that?

Oh, well, I guess the first batch of records, because that was before I had a manager, you know. And of course when Carlos Gastel came into the picture -- we're getting a little ahead in this, because I'm even getting ahead of how I got -- how I got recognized.

No, we haven't covered that yet. But since we're talking about the record bit, you know, I'm just saying that what used to happen is you'd get paid so much money for a record, you know. Like today, they're called demo records today. Well, this is what they used to do. They'd pay you so much to do a record, you see, a flat thing, you see, like to get started. And then of course they would tell you, they'd say, well, if the record is a success, if it does well, then you'll get a royalty contract. Now, this is what they --
But if it does well, if it sells a million copies, you won't get anything. You'll get a contract to do the next one.
Yeah, see. So this is what they promised

you, see, but they promised me that I would get a royalty contract, see. "If this record is a hit you'll get a royalty." Because when somebody would come up and say, "Listen, I want you to do this thing for me, and we're going to pay you --," say for instance $100.00, or, "We'll pay you a hundred bucks a tune," you know. Well, this of course you look at it two different ways, you know, particularly when you are experienced as I was. I wasn't a greenhorn at all, because I'd been around since I was a kid. And this was a new venture for me, getting into the record business, you know, being recognized as a recording artist was a completely different thing, as I say, before, than what I had planned to get into. No doubt if I had planned to get into that I would have, -- you know, I would have done it a little different. I would have --

But anyway, when the opportunity did come about, well, like with many people, you say, well, I'll give it a try. It's just like a trial thing, but it doesn't end up being a trial, that's what I'm trying to say.

It doesn't end up being -- somebody's not fair enough to say, well, you know, you made it, and now we're going to let you make yours, see. But the way the thing was at that time, you ended up always owing the record company. Even the records, as many records as I made, according to the record companies I still owe the record companies.
